You might have again a few reads and
reviews from friends and family and
people who care about you, but typically
a first book is not going to skyrocket
any of us to success. Most of us are not
special unicorns and we're not going to
just put out a book and suddenly be
making all this money and have all this
success and suddenly we're, you know,
quitting our full-time jobs to be
full-time authors. That's probably not
going to happen. So, if you can go into
publishing your first book or even your
first few books with the understanding
that that is unlikely to be the kind of
trajectory of your author career, then
you can set yourself up for success and
you can kind of temper those
expectations so that you don't feel let
down or frustrated or disappointed when
your book comes out. I have said it
before and I will keep saying it.
Self-publishing is a long game and if
you want to succeed in self-publishing,
I feel that you have to have grit, you
have to have consistency, and you have
to think long-term. You can't think
short-sighted. You can't constantly be
thinking short-term and just vying for
the next sparkly thing. It's really
a process of building an entire career
around publishing. Every single review,
every single new reader that you get on
your arc team, every single newsletter
subscriber, it builds, and these things
compound over time. So, if you go into
publishing already with the mindset of
this will probably be slow. My growth is
going to be slow, but I'm going to be
consistent. I'm going to dig deep even
on those hard days, and I'm going to
keep doing this because I love it, and I
want to build a a career out of this,
then you're going to be setting yourself
up for success rather than hoping for
this really sparkly kind of short-term
viral success that might not happen, and
then you feel like you're let down.
Maybe then, you know, you're not sure
you want to keep doing this. Maybe you
burn yourself out. Any of those things
could happen. But, I find that when
you shift your thinking to long-term, it
helps you to feel a lot more grateful
for all the good things that come your
way. It helps to look at the business as
something, again, that compounds over
time. This isn't a get-rich-quick
scheme. There are those creators that
you will see out there who really tout,
like, just do this, and suddenly you're
going to be making all this money
writing books. But, for those of us who
are really in it for the stories, and
we're in it for the heart and the soul
of storytelling, this is not
get-rich-quick. This is not get famous
and be a superstar quick. This is not
suddenly everybody's going to read your
book, and you're going to be a household
name. This is difficult. Every aspect of
self-publishing is difficult. But again,
if you go into it with that mindset
already, knowing it's going to be
difficult, knowing it's going to take
time, but enjoying it and loving it and
even, you know, loving the
the difficult days as well and being
okay with those, then I do feel you will
be a lot more successful in the long
term versus somebody who just wants to
get famous on social media for a book
that they wrote and when it doesn't
happen, they feel so disappointed that
they stop writing and never return to
their books. So, those are the five
mistakes that I have made and that I
have seen other self-publishers make. I
do hope this video will help you to
avoid some of these pitfalls, avoid some
of these mistakes. I would also love to

and we therefore are going to be

readability now I do have um I printed
out here
some quotes from Chicago the Chicago
Manual of style is the style guide that
we use for our fiction so this is
Chicago's preference for capitalization
proper nouns are usually capitalized as
are some of the terms derived from or
associated with proper nouns for the
latter Chicago's preference is for
sparing use of capitals which is
sometimes referred to as down style and
that is from CMOS 8.1 if you have the
Chicago Manual of style and are
interested in looking that up so where
does this question of whether or not to
cap a term really come from I believe it
comes from two places and the first
which I've already mentioned is when an
author is making up their own terms or
creatures or what have you and they
don't know whether or not that made-up
term should be capitalized since it is

where I see this happening is when a
term a word carries weight and it

I see capitalized all the time that
would fall under this category of you

those are the two reasons that we

Natalia said that right there is your

book that you're working on what I would
recommend is to write the first draft
and don't think too much about character
development or characterization I know
that a lot of people like to print out
you know entire packets of like
character questions and develop their
characters before they start writing
them but that has never worked for me
because I can I can plan out who a
character is on paper but then as soon
as I start telling their story or as
soon as they start telling their story
to me which is often what it feels like
I will usually discover that that
character is very different than the way
I made them out to be on paper when I
was filling in the character
questionnaire so my first draft now at
this point my first draft is learning
who the characters are and allowing them
to tell me their story allowing them to
show me who they are
and then in multiple rounds of revisions
I'm able to kind of unearth that and I'm
able to polish their personality and
really bring them to life in an
authentic way and that just takes time
and it takes multiple rounds of revision
and I also think it kind of takes just
being brave being brave enough to let
your character tell their story and
letting your character be authentic many
people would probably think I'm crazy to
hear me talk like this but I'm sure you
writers out there understand how it
feels when a character really is telling
their own story like I don't believe
that I created Daisy
so my
as she came to life and told me her
story on her own so when I became brave
enough to let her be her authentic self
then I feel her character just jumped
off the page and her story became much
more truthful from that point forward so
take your time don't be in a rush you
know don't feel like you have to fill
out a questionnaire that's 500 questions
long to figure out who your character is
let them develop over the course of
multiple drafts because what I often
discover and what I think you'll
discover as well is if the character you
know who we think our characters should
be is not always who those characters
actually are and by letting them be
themselves I think you'll be allowing
your readers to better connect with your
characters and better connect with your
story and really get pulled in and feel
like the storytelling experience has
been an immersive experience for them
which is what we're all kind of aiming
for when we're telling stories so thank
you guys so much for being here today
and for listening to my seven tips for
writing strong and complex characters if
you have any questions you can always
leave them in the comments down below
I'm always open to suggestions for video
topics and if you didn't already know I

and my business enchanted ink publishing

I hope you are all doing well I hope you

number one you need to give your

to have something that they're working

something there's something standing in

something really bad really nasty

something had better come from that door

there is a gun in a scene the gun had
better go off you know it's not just
sitting there to be a prop it needs to
be used and suspense is dependent on
that it's dependent on the small details
and bits of information that you're
giving your readers that promise
something and from there you have to
make sure that you keep your promise and
you see it all the way through to the
end and with suspense that doesn't mean
that it has to be immediately in that
scene with the example I gave you that
door being unlocked that is a kind of
short period of suspense because this
character is ultimately going to leave
the house again and realize oh the door
was unlocked so that promise will need
to be kept pretty damn quick after that
happens probably that night when she
crawls into bed and her door is unlocked
depending on the story you're telling
and the types of suspense that you're
trying to weave into your narrative
there can be larger promises that really

the climax of your novel
for example maybe there's a bomb that's

different timeline
and timeframes that you can use to play

Hello everybody. My name is Natalia Lee
and I'm the author of the young adult
novels Highborn and Way of Spears. And
today I'm going to be talking to you
about filtering. What is it? What are
some examples of it and how do you avoid
it in your manuscript? Let's just get
started.
So for the longest time, I had no idea
that filtering was even a thing. I think
I first
found out that it was a thing to look
out for while I was reading through some
like freelance editors pages and they
were talking about what they really
focused on finding within a manuscript
that they were working with and a lot of
them mentioned filtering and I had no
idea what they were talking about. So I
avoided it for a while cuz I was like,
you know, I don't want to add another
thing into my brain that I have to focus
on while I'm writing a draft. But now
I'm on the third draft of my novel Song
of the Dryad and my beta readers have
graciously pointed out to me that I have
been filtering a lot in my novel. So
what even is filtering?
The way I understand it and I'm going to
give you my descriptions. If you want to
go look up a Google definition, go ahead
and do that. But I'm just going to
explain it to you in the way that I
understand in the way that I
um
interact with it. So to me filtering
means that I am kind of putting up a
veil between the action and the
character and the reader. So the reader
isn't really experiencing the action
with the character so much as hearing
about it afterwards or just being told
about it. So in a way it can also have a
you know, telling versus showing type
characteristic to it.
So an example might be um if I was
filtering, I might say
Charlotte felt Charlotte is the main
character of my novel by the way um and
she hikes through the forest a lot. So I
might say something like Charlotte felt
the you know, the wind on her cheeks. So
that would be an example of filtering
because I'm saying Charlotte felt X. You
know, she felt this thing. Rather than
saying, you know, Charlotte lifted her
head and the breeze played through her
hair.
Now that is really throwing you directly
into the action. You're experiencing the
lifting of the head. You're experiencing
the wind blowing through her hair and
it's really more immersive than just
saying Charlotte felt the wind on her
face. You know, that is really
taking the reader and pushing them away.
You know, you get to observe this action
rather than experiencing it alongside
the character. So that's you know,
that's kind of my understanding of it.
Now as I've been going through my
manuscript um like I said, I have had
betas pointing it out to me, but now I
have a sharp enough eye to catch it on
my own even when my betas have missed
it. So I do it a lot um
Charlotte felt this. Charlotte heard
that. Charlotte saw this. So it's like I
I was using my senses. You know, I was
using the five senses, but I was using
them in a way that removed the reader
from the action of the novel rather than
immersing them in it. And
really what I'm going for here with my
novel is a fully immersive experience. I
really want readers to feel like they
are right there alongside with my
character walking hand in hand with her
experiencing what's going on in the
novel rather than feeling like they're
hovering at a distance watching. And
filtering can absolutely make readers
feel like they're being held at a
distance. So again, I picture it like a
veil.
Instead of the reader being right there,
there's a little veil between them and
the action that they're having to kind
of peer through and that's what
filtering means to me. Um again, this
was something that I didn't know much
about even you know, two months ago. So
when I was writing the first draft, I
had no idea what filtering was. When I
finished the second draft, I still had
no idea what filtering was, but I see it
now and I'm so grateful that my betas
pointed it out to me because now that I
am
editing all of the filtering out of my
novel, I feel like the the action is so
much more powerful because
you're actually there with Charlotte and
experiencing that the these things that
she's experiencing rather than being
told about them. Uh so again, like I
said before, this to me is kind of an
example of me telling the reader that
something's happening rather than
showing the reader what's happening. And
I try to go for showing the reader
what's happening as often as possible.
Now
it's it's not like
you can never filter in your novel.
There are absolutely sometimes where I
go to fix a segment of filtering and I

instances
filtering really works the best within

## BETA READER Q&A

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GTBqLfJHF6Y>
Caption file: GTBqLfJHF6Y.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Editing & Revision
Secondary Topics: Genre, Reader Experience & Engagement
Tertiary Topics: Beta Readers, Feedback, Genre Conventions, Filtering, Scene Craft, Motivation, Motivation & Desire, Deadlines

Hello everybody. My name is Natalia Lee
and I'm the author of the young adult
novels Highborn and Wave Spears and
today I am bringing you my beta reader
Q&A. What I'm going to do is I'm just
going to say the first name of the
person that asked the question because
there were some beautiful last names
that I know I'm not going to be able to
pronounce correctly. So rather than
butchering those, I'm just going to say
the first name of the person who asked
the question. So let's just jump right
into it.
[Music]
Okay, so the first question is from
Emily and Emily asks, "Hey Natalia, I
was wondering if you asked your betas
any questions. For example, if you had
any issues with a character or setting

I like the idea of handing over a whole
manuscript but I'd also like to focus on
the parts I want the feedback on or do
you find them giving feedback as the
opinions come to them more beneficial
because it's part of their experience?"
So I did give my betas guided questions.
So the way I did this was I put the
guided questions at the end of every
chapter and then as far as, you know, do
do I find that my betas giving feedback
as the opinions come to them is more
beneficial?
I'd say yes and no. Yes because I want
to know what my betas are actually
thinking and feeling while they're
reading and I know that by asking
certain questions I'm triggering certain

I'm asking questions about the things

I'd say you can go both ways on this. Um

Hello everybody. My name is Natalia Lee,
and I'm the author of the young adult
novels Highborn and Wave Speakers. And

50,000 words in a month. And I'm hoping

much as possible during the first week
of NaNoWriMo. The first week is when you
are going to be most excited about your
project and most excited about
NaNoWriMo. So you should utilize all of
that energy and inspiration and write as
much as possible. Because once week two
and three roll around, your inspiration
is probably going to kind of plummet,
your energy is going to fall, and you
are not going to be as excited about
writing 50,000 words in a month. So try
to get ahead of your word count goal in
that first seven days in order to help

to participate in word sprints and
community events. Word sprints are
really helpful for me, especially during
NaNoWriMo, because they force me to
focus on one thing, which is writing,
for a set amount of time. If I tried to
do a word sprint that's too long, then I
end up getting distracted by my phone or
the computer or talking to somebody
that's at the house. But if I set a, you
know, a watch timer for myself and I
say, "Okay, I'm going to write for 5
minutes, and that's all I'm going to
do." Or 10 minutes, or 15, then I'm able
to dedicate that 15 minutes to writing
only, and I get a a done.

1 to be one of the most diffult chapters
to write just because you're starting a
new story with a bunch of new characters
that you might not know very well or if
you're writing a sequel or a series yes
you know these characters but it's a
completely new story and there's a lot
writing on chapter one so it can
definitely feel intimidating but just

writing it and know that you can always
rewrite it or come back and edit it
later my second tip is to start chapter
1 and to start your novel near the
inciting incident no reader wants to
pick up a book and then have to read 10
chapters before they even figure out
what the inciting incident is and if you
don't know what an inciting incident is
it is the thing that happens to trigger
the rest of the story so in Harry Potter
for example it would be getting the
letter that invites him to Hogwarts or
maybe meeting Hagrid is the inciting
incident depending on how you want to
look at it but it is that trigger that
starts all of the events in motion so
you want to start chapter 1 near that
event uh as close to it as possible some
people even start with the inciting
incident but just know that you don't
want to keep your readers waiting too
long to give them that little tidbit of
information that tells them what the
story is going to be about and gets them
on the role with the action my third tip

Us in the reality of the novel so start

## HOW TO BE A GREAT CRITIQUE PARTNER

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9GgjAnlGifQ>
Caption file: 9GgjAnlGifQ.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Editing & Revision
Secondary Topics: Character, Genre, Writing Craft
Tertiary Topics: Feedback, Critique Partners, Revision, Beta Readers, Motivation & Desire, Social Media, Writing Habits

hello everybody my name is Natalia Lee
and I'm the author of the young adult
novels Highborn and way of Spears and
today I'm going to be chatting with you
about how you can be the best critique
partner you can be let's get
started so to begin with I want to start
off by telling you a bit of my
experience with having critique Partners
not only have I written two novels in
the past and I worked with critique
Partners on those but I also made
majored in English with a concentration
in creative writing when I was in
college and my creative writing classes
were comprised primarily of receiving
and giving critiques so I was critiquing
people every single week multiple times
a week and I was also being critiqued
regularly every semester so I have a
pretty good idea about how this goes so
with my experience out of the way let's
go ahead and talk about how you can be
an amazing critique partner so first up
you should be extreme careful about time
management to begin with if you are the
writer and you are giving your work to
your critique Partners be very clear
about when you would like to get that
work back many of us are very busy and
don't have time to just sit down and
focus on one project so if you're
expecting your critique partner to get
their notes and revisions back to you
within say a week or two weeks make sure
to let them know because if they don't
know that they might be planning on
getting it back to you in 3 weeks or 6
weeks so if you don't have this already
figured out this can lead to a lot of
frustration down the road and you and
your critique partner might kind of butt
heads about it so make sure that both of
you are clear about when you want to
give revisions and when you want to
receive them back now this is a bad
habit that many of us have and that is
procrastination but if you are working
with an author and you are their
critique partner they're going to be
extremely dependent on you to be getting
your notes back to them in a timely
manner which means you should not
procrastinate procrastinate is just
going to lead to frustration and then
you won't be looking at your partner's
work with a clear and focused mind which
is what I want to talk about next so
first up make sure that you ask your
critique partner what they're looking
for and what their goals are you don't
want to approach a piece of work
thinking that the author wants to
publish it when really they just want to
send it in a letter or maybe post it on
their blog so you need to know what
platform they're using and what they
plan to do with that work before you can
clearly critique it next up and this
goes along with don't procrastinate is
to make sure that you are reading your
partner's work and making your notes
when you're very focused and have a
clear head if you are behind on notes
and your critique partner is getting
frustrated this is going to force you to
rush and then you're not going to do
your best work so make sure that you are
not procrastinating you are focusing and
you are not rushing this is the best way
to really give your critique partner
your best self and your best work now
this next tip is something that I used
to struggle with because I love grammar
I love spelling and what I used to do
was Circle every misspelling and every
grammatical error in the work that I was
critiquing but I found that that was
incredibly unhelpful to my partners
because they would often end up changing
large sections of their work anyway so
all of those notes I'd written about
spelling errors weren't helpful and it
was just kind of tedious for me to do
and tedious for the author to read
through and it wasn't appreciated in the
long run if your critique partner is
consistently making an error or spelling
something wrong then you can certainly
note that so that they can make sure
that they're not doing that from that
point forward but to go through the
entire manuscript and just circle all
the misspelled words is going to be a
waste of your time I'm filming a video
so instead of focusing on all of those
small mechanics try to focus on the
bigger picture like plot and characters
my next tip is to give your critique
partner objective feedback rather than
subjective feedback subjective feedback
is based more specifically on your
preferences and opinions rather than the
weaknesses in the author's writing so an
example of objective feedback would be
this character seems one-dimensional to
me and I believe this is how you could
fix that that would be objective but
subjective would be I don't like this
character and I think she's stupid so
you should remove her do you see the big
difference there and how one could be
incredibly helpful while the other would
just be be frustrating to the author
next up let's talk about how to deliver
criticism because this is something that
not all of us have practiced with and we
need to learn how to do it in a way that
will be beneficial to the writer without
tearing them down and beating them up
about it some of us have experienced
with receiving harsh criticism and if

know how bad it feels when you give
somebody your work something that's
incredibly close to your heart and they
rip it apart it's one thing to give
criticis ISM that is beneficial and
helpful it's something else to give
criticism that kind of Nags at the

## ALL ABOUT CRITIQUE PARTNERS

Primary Topic: Editing & Revision
Secondary Topics: Scene Craft, Genre, Reader Experience & Engagement

hello everybody my name is Natalia Lee
and I'm the author of the young adult
novels Highborn and way of Spears and
today we are going to be chatting all
about critique Partners let's get
started so the first question I want to
tackle is what is a critique partner a
critique partner is a fellow writer who
helps make your work the best that it
can be because your critique partner is
a writer they're going to go over your
work with much more scrutiny than a beta
reader would a beta reader is reading
your work in search of entertainment
while a critique partner is looking for
plot holes character inconsistencies and
other technical aspects of the
storytelling process the second question
is how does it work so this is going to
depend on you and your critique partner
you might want to exchange one chapter a
day five chapters a week or maybe one
large chunk of your story every month
this is all going to depend on how much
time you have how fast you work and what
your deadline is now keep in mind that
your critique partner may be working on
their own novel or short story at the
same time that they're helping you with
yours so don't go into this partnership
thinking that you will just be getting
feedback on your work you also need to
be willing to put time and effort into
looking over your critique partner's
work as well when I was looking for
critique partners for way of Spears I
specifically went out looking for
writers that were in the same point in
their Ting process for their novels as I
was so that we could have a mutually
beneficial critique partner relationship
it's not that I was handing out my novel
and my critique Partners were only
giving me feedback I would give them
five chapters of my book and then they
would give me five chapters of their
book so this was I feel like this was a
really good way to work it because after
you give your critique partner your
chapters you're really looking forward
to getting their feedback and in all
that and fcy time that I was waiting to
hear back from them I was able to work
on their chapters and make all of my
notes and edits which I really enjoy
doing so it ended up working out really
well for us so after your critique
partner receives your chapter or
chapters they will read it and make
extensive notes these notes are meant to
help you and be beneficial while you are
going through the editing process after
making all their notes they're going to
return your document to you you can use
word or Google Docs like I used or if
you prefer face to- face interaction you
can do the whole paper and red pen thing
the next question is where do I find a

different places where you can find
somebody that is going to be able to
help you with your writing but first ask
yourself do you want somebody that you
can sit down with in person or would you
prefer online correspondence if you
would prefer face-to-face interaction
you can seek out your peers in your
creative writing shop you can take
writing workshops at your local
community college or local library or or
maybe you even want to post an ad
somewhere I have actually seen ads for
critique Partners in coffee shops and
what I have seen I've never tried this
but I have seen the the whole thing
where you like cut up the bottom of the
paper so you leave just your name and
your number on it and then if somebody's
interested in working with you and
working with your writing they can just
give you a call now personally I have a
bit of social anxiety so I definitely do
not want to go out and meet a stranger
and sit down with them and let them read

correspondence and believe me when I say
that meeting somebody online is so much

creative work so that when you come back

the street? Do they smell exhaust fumes
like I would smell if I went walking
down the street outside the house, or
are they going to smell yeast and
freshly baked bread because they're
walking through a market square? What
are the kinds of things that they're

sensory details are extremely important
when you're building a world because it
makes the reader feel like they can dive

there with your characters. My third tip
is to spend a lot of time getting to
know the culture of your world. There
there's a lot that goes into culture. Um
for example,
you'll want to know the religion,
traditions, the rituals, the belief

to have figured out before you writing
this novel. How How does the magic work?

feed the horses make sure everybody was

and then write again and then I would
typically have to go to class work
during the day get all of my chores done

small blocks of time in which I could
write and that really helped me now
within those small blocks of time I
really likeed to do word Sprints now
what a word Sprint is is a scheduled
amount of time it might be 10 minutes 20
minutes 30 minutes it depends on who is
holding the word Sprint and during that
amount of time you write as much as
possible and you don't look back so once
you hit the end of the Sprint you have a
bunch of words because typically you're
kind of racing against the clock
yourself and other people and then you
will post the amount of words you had
when you done and that always got me a
bunch of words sometimes I would write
500 words per Sprint and that leads into
my other tip which is to stop frequently
I stop every 500 Words I write so even
if I have 30 minutes of time let's say I

I'll get up and go do something else for
the rest of those 15 minutes I don't
force myself to sit there and write for
for a regularly scheduled amount of time

just make sure you have it somewhere

another tip is when you stop writing at
the end of the day or at the end of a
session try to stop writing at a
